answers.step: Basic syntax: variables, data types, and simple operations
answers.content:
[source 1] The interpreter acts as a simple calculator: you can type an expression into it and it will write the value.  
[source 1] Expression syntax is straightforward: the operators +, -, * and / can be used to perform arithmetic; parentheses (()) can be used for grouping.  
[source 1] For example:  
[source 1] ```  
>>> 2 + 2  
4  
>>> 50 - 5*6  
20  
>>> (50 - 5*6) / 4  
5.0  
>>> 8 / 5  # division always returns a floating-point number  
1.6  
```  
[source 1] The equal sign (=) is used to assign a value to a variable.  
[source 1] Afterwards, no result is displayed before the next interactive prompt:  
[source 1] ```  
>>> width = 20  
>>> height = 5 * 9  
>>> width * height  
900  
```  
[source 1] In interactive mode, the last printed expression is assigned to the variable _.  
[source 1] This means that when you are using Python as a desk calculator, it is somewhat easier to continue calculations, for example:  
[source 1] ```  
>>> tax = 12.5 / 100  
>>> price = 100.50  
>>> price * tax  
12.5625  
>>> price + _  
113.0625  
>>> round(_, 2)  
113.06  
```  
[source 1] Python can manipulate text (represented by type str, so-called “strings”) as well as numbers.  
[source 1] This includes characters “!”, words “rabbit”, names “Paris”, sentences “Got your back.”, etc.  
[source 1] “Yay! :)”. They can be enclosed in single quotes ('...') or double quotes ("...") with the same result.  
[source 1] ```  
>>> 'spam eggs'  # single quotes  
'spam eggs'  
>>> "Paris rabbit got your back :)! Yay!"  # double quotes  
'Paris rabbit got your back :)! Yay!'  
>>> '1975'  # digits and numerals enclosed in quotes are also strings  
'1975'  
```  
[source 2] A variable is a name attached to a value. In Python you create one simply by assigning with = — there is no separate declaration, and you never write the type yourself:  
[source 2] ```  
age = 27  
price = 9.99  
name = "Grace"  
is_student = True  
nothing = None  
```  
[source 2] Python figures out the type from the value on the right.  
[source 2] You can check it at any time with type():  
[source 2] ```  
print(type(age))  
print(type(price))  
print(type(name))  
print(type(is_student))  
```  
[source 2] A variable can later point at a different value — even one of a different type.  
[source 2] This is called dynamic typing and it is one of the reasons Python code is short.  
[source 2] Names contain letters, digits and underscores, and cannot start with a digit: total_2 is fine, 2total is a syntax error.  
[source 2] Names are case-sensitive: score, Score and SCORE are three different variables.  
[source 2] You cannot use Python's 35 keywords (if, for, class, None…) as names.  
[source 2] Convention (PEP 8): use snake_case for variables and functions, UPPER_CASE for constants, CamelCase for classes.  
[source 2] int42, -7, 10**100Whole numbers of any size — Python integers never overflow.  
[source 2] str"hi", 'hi', """multi-line"""Text, Unicode by default.  
[source 2] NoneTypeNone"No value" — the default return of a function that returns nothing.  
[source 3] A variable is something that we use to hold a value.  
[source 3] We can create are own variables that hold and store values by typing a variable name and then setting it equal to a certain data type (see below).  
[source 3] A valid variable name is anything that does not start with a number and contains only letters and underscores (NO SPACES).  
[source 3] Capitals in variable names are allowed but do make a difference: the variable tim is NOT the same variable as Tim.  
[source 3] ```  
tim = "hello"  
myVariable = True  
```  
[source 3] To reference our variables we simply type their name.  
[source 3] We can easily change variables that already exist by typing that variable name and then setting it equal to a new value.  
[source 3] ```  
tim = "hello"  
myVariable = True  
myVariable = 3  # myVariable now is equal to 3  
joe = myVariable  # joe is now equal to 3 because myVariable has the value 3  
```  
[source 3] To display something to the shell in python we can use the keyword "print":  
[source 3] ```  
var = "hello"  
print("hi")  
print(var)  # This will print "hello"  
```
